transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Avery Lin (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (ClearSight Head of ML), Daniel Kim (Eng Manager), Sofia Martinez (CTO)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood, and with me is Marcus our senior SE. Appreciate you taking the time, Priya, Daniel, Sofia. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the quant stuff - we've been wrestling with latency vs accuracy on our generation pipelines.
[00:13] Daniel: Yeah we've got a hard p99 SLAs for some user-facing flows so curious about tradeoffs.
[00:18] Marcus: Great, we'll jump in. Quick agenda: show Optimize's quantization profiles (INT8/FP8), share quality vs latency charts, then discuss how a pilot would look and next steps.
[00:28] Sofia: Sounds good. Also want to confirm security and deployment options later.

--- Quick intro + context gathering ---
[00:35] Avery: Priya, can you give a 2-minute overview of your stack and what "success" looks like?
[00:42] Priya: Sure. We're on k8s in GCP, using a mix of open models - mostly fine-tuned Llama variants and a couple of LLMs for embeddings. Production traffic: a mixture of high-throughput batched jobs and low-latency interactive queries. Success is meeting p50/p95 latency targets under 200ms for interactive flows and keeping generation quality within 3% of our baseline human eval metric. Also cost per 1k tokens matters.
[01:05] Avery: Great, that helps. We're going to focus on quant profiles and how Redwood Optimize recommends INT8 or FP8 per-model / per-workload.

--- Demo: Quantization profiles ---
[01:18] Marcus: (screen share) Here is the Optimize console. Top-level: recommended quant profile - we call it a profile because it's a bundle of kernel choices, per-layer quantization, and calibration thresholds. For this customer we've pre-run a few jobs and you can see two candidate profiles: INT8-standard and FP8-high.
[01:35] Marcus: INT8-standard gives ~2.8x lower VRAM and usably lower latency, FP8-high keeps more dynamic range and typically preserves quality better on instruction-following tasks.
[01:45] Priya: Quick question - when you say FP8, are we talking about bfloat-ish FP8 or the new E4M3 format?
[01:51] Marcus: Good call - we support E4M3 and E5M2 variants depending on the deployment hardware. On A100s we tend to use E4M3; on some upcoming HW we evaluate E5M2. Optimization picks the format per-node. (small stutter) apologies, autocaption says E-pm3 that's a transcribe error - but key is hardware-led variant selection.

[02:12] Marcus: Now the chart - quality vs latency. X-axis is median latency (ms) for a 512-token sequence, Y-axis is quality delta vs FP32 baseline measured on your prompt set (higher is better). INT8 tends to drop quality 1.5-3% but reduces latency ~30-45%. FP8 is usually within 0.5-1.5% quality delta and reduces latency ~15-25%.
[02:36] Daniel: Those percentages are aggregated - can we see per-prompt or per-instruction breakdowns? Some of our prompts are long context heavy and we care about p99 latency.
[02:44] Marcus: Yes, Optimize stores per-prompt deltas and latency distributions. Here's the per-prompt table - you can filter by instruction length and see the small subset where INT8 fails more often on truthfulness metrics.

[03:05] Priya: We're sensitive to hallucination increase even at 1%. Any examples?
[03:10] Marcus: (narrating) Example: on a retrieval-augmented prompt with many numeric tokens, INT8 had a higher token-repeat or number drop in ~2 of 1500 samples. FP8 preserved those values in our runs.
[03:23] Priya: Ok. So FP8 looks safer for critical flows, INT8 for cost-sensitive bulk jobs.

--- Technical deep dive and caveats ---
[03:30] Marcus: A few important things: caching and KV cache behavior matters. For many interactive flows we keep KV cache hot and that actually reduces the relative penalty of FP32 vs quantized runs, because recomputation is smaller. For long-context batch jobs INT8's memory wins are more pronounced.
[03:50] Marcus: Also we select kernels per-layer - some attention layers quantize poorly, Optimize will keep those layers in FP16/FP32 while quantizing the rest; that's why we call it a profile rather than all-or-nothing.
[04:02] Daniel: Nice. How do you handle fallback if we see quality regressions in production?
[04:07] Avery: Two things: routing and rollouts. You can route by policy (latency cost) and do a canary where 5-10% of traffic uses FP32/FP16 fallback; Optimize flags regressions based on your evaluation set and can auto-failover to the safer profile.

[04:20] Sofia: Deployment-wise we prefer dedicated nodes for predictable p99. Thoughts?
[04:25] Marcus: Dedicated helps with tail latency consistency; plus you can pin hardware that supports specific FP8 formats. We can provision Dedicated capacity and run the pilot there.

--- Numbers and benchmark examples ---
[04:35] Marcus: Here's a concrete example from a similar customer: model X (30B), FP32 baseline median latency 420ms for 512 tokens. INT8 profile median 240ms, p99 520ms. FP8 profile median 320ms, p99 380ms. Quality delta: INT8 -2.6% per our eval rubric, FP8 -0.7%.
[04:58] Priya: Those p99 numbers are critical - INT8 p99 looks worse there, interestingly. Why?
[05:03] Marcus: It's due to kernel fallback and occasional dequantization hotspots on long layers; we mitigate with autoscaling and batching heuristics but p99 can spike. That's why we recommend canaries for interactive flows.

[05:18] Daniel: On the cost side, do you have unit economics?
[05:21] Avery: Yes - for that model the cost per 1k tokens on Hosted was $0.12 FP32, INT8 was roughly $0.045, FP8 around $0.07, numbers vary by region/hardware. We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet with raw logs so you can plug your prompt distribution.

--- Customer questions / objections ---
[05:40] Priya: How intrusive is the calibration step? We need to keep PII off dev logging.
[05:45] Marcus: Calibration can run on a sample set you provide in-situ; it's optional to send transcripts externally. We also support a private deployment where calibration runs inside your VPC. For SOC 2/data residency we can restrict artifacts.
[05:58] Sofia: We use SAML SSO and have strict RBAC. Any blockers?
[06:03] Avery: We support SAML, SCIM provisioning, fine-grained RBAC, audit logs; we'll share the security pack - SOC 2 report and deployment checklist.

--- Pilot scope discussion ---
[06:12] Daniel: For the pilot, we'd like to test both INT8 and FP8 on a dedicated pool with our prompt set and measure p50/p95/p99 and quality metrics. Two-week pilot ok?
[06:20] Marcus: Yes, two weeks is typical. We'll provision nodes and give you access to Optimize dashboards and raw traces. We'll also run a calibration pass and save profiles.
[06:29] Priya: Can we do A/B routing to split traffic for canary?
[06:32] Avery: Absolutely. We can set up canary routing rules, and you'll see per-route cost/lambda breakdown.

--- Administrative details + timeline ---
[06:40] Marcus: For the pilot we'll need: sample prompt set (Priya), expected QPS and p99 targets (Daniel), and a list of models to test. We can have configs ready in 48 hours once we have assets.
[06:52] Priya: We'll share prompts and metrics by Friday.
[06:55] Avery: Great. We'll also send the benchmark spreadsheet and pricing, and the SOC2/security docs.

--- Closing recap ---
[07:02] Avery: Quick recap: 1) INT8 gives biggest cost and memory wins but has higher quality risk for some prompts and can cause p99 spikes; 2) FP8 is middle ground with better quality preservation; 3) Redwood Optimize picks per-layer profiles and can do mixed precision; 4) We'll provision a 2-week dedicated pilot, send spreadsheets and security docs, schedule a technical deep dive next week.
[07:24] Sofia: That works for us. Looking forward to the pilot.
[07:28] Priya: Thanks both - this was useful.
[07:31] Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the assets and meeting invite.
[07:35] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript transcription has occasional mislabels and auto-caption errors (e.g., E-pm3). Links referenced during call: "quant-bench-CLRS.xlsx" (to be shared), "redwood-security-pack.pdf" (to be shared).
